questions.q: What is the recommended first step before running `pip install qiskit qiskit-aer qiskit-ibm-runtime`?
options: Uninstall all other Python versions on the machine
Create and activate an isolated virtual environment (via `venv` or `conda`)
Create an IBM Quantum Platform account
Install `qiskit-algorithms` first, since the others depend on it
questions.explain: Installing into an isolated virtual environment avoids version conflicts with other projects and makes your setup reproducible. The IBM account is only needed later, for real-hardware access.

questions.q: How do you verify that the core Qiskit install worked?
options: Run `qiskit --test` from the command line
Import it and print its version: `import qiskit; print(qiskit.__version__)`
Check that `qiskit-ibm-runtime` imports, since it implies the core package is installed too
There is no way to verify an install without running a circuit on real hardware
questions.explain: Importing `qiskit` and printing `qiskit.__version__` is the standard, immediate way to confirm the package is installed and importable in your active environment.

questions.q: What do you get from your IBM Quantum Platform account dashboard that you need for `save_account`?
options: A downloadable local simulator binary
A Jupyter notebook template
An API token and an instance identifier (such as an instance CRN)
A pre-transpiled circuit file
questions.explain: The dashboard provides the API token and instance/CRN identifier used to authenticate `QiskitRuntimeService.save_account` against your account.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against treating the exact `channel` value and token flow shown in `save_account` as permanently fixed?
options: Because `save_account` is deprecated and no longer works at all
Because IBM has changed its cloud authentication flow and channel naming over time, so current docs are the real source of truth
Because the token value changes automatically every 24 hours
Because `save_account` only works inside Jupyter, never in VS Code
questions.explain: IBM's cloud auth and channel naming have evolved as the platform matured. The lesson is honest that you should check IBM's current documentation rather than assume any one snippet, including its own, stays accurate forever.

questions.q: What is a common cause of `import qiskit` failing in Jupyter even after a successful `pip install`?
options: Qiskit simply cannot be imported from inside Jupyter under any circumstances
The Jupyter kernel is tied to a different Python environment than the one you installed into
Jupyter requires a separate paid license to import third-party packages
`qiskit-aer` must be imported before `qiskit` or the import always fails
questions.explain: A very common mistake is activating one virtual environment in a terminal while the Jupyter kernel actually running your notebook is tied to a different environment (or the system Python), so the install never reaches the kernel's `import` path.
